learnings.title: Top-Down Traversal, Bottom-Up Construction
learnings.answer:
A reusable recursion pattern for nested **objects and arrays**: traverse **down** into children first, then **build a new structure upward** from what each recursive call returns.

Instead of modifying the input in place, build a **new array or object at each recursive step**. This avoids sparse-array holes from `delete` and keeps the logic much easier to follow.

## The two phases

| Phase | What you do |
| --- | --- |
| **Top-down traversal** | Recurse into each nested child **before** deciding what to keep or transform at the current level |
| **Bottom-up construction** | At each level, assemble a **fresh** container from values returned by calls below |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph topDown [Top-down traversal]
    visit[Visit node] --> recurse[Recurse into each child first]
  end
  subgraph bottomUp [Bottom-up construction]
    receive[Receive returned values] --> build[Build new container from children]
    build --> returnNode[Return new structure upward]
  end
  recurse --> receive
```

**Golden rule:** never mutate the input tree in place — always return a newly built structure.

## Generic recursive skeleton

```javascript
function transform(node) {
  if (isBaseCase(node)) return node;        // stop traversal

  const result = newContainer();            // bottom-up: fresh container

  for (const child of children(node)) {
    const processed = transform(child);     // top-down: recurse first
    if (shouldKeep(processed)) {
      add(result, processed);               // bottom-up: assemble
    }
  }

  return result;
}
```

- `transform(child)` → **top-down** (go deeper before assembling this level)
- `newContainer()` + `add(result, …)` → **bottom-up** (build from returned children)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  start[Enter transform node] --> base{Base case?}
  base -->|primitive or null| returnAsIs[Return node as-is]
  base -->|object or array| newEmpty[Create empty new container]
  newEmpty --> loop[For each child value]
  loop --> callRecurse["Top-down: processed = transform(child)"]
  callRecurse --> keep{shouldKeep processed?}
  keep -->|no| loop
  keep -->|yes| addChild["Bottom-up: add processed to container"]
  addChild --> loop
  loop --> returnBuilt[Return new container]
```

## When to use this pattern

- Filtering or mapping nested JSON trees
- Deep copy, flatten, or compact nested structures
- Any problem where input is a tree of objects/arrays and output has the same shape (or a flattened/diffed variant)

## Leaf vs branch — the JSON / object manipulation category

This exact **leaf vs branch** recursive framework is the secret to solving almost the entire **JSON / object manipulation** category of interview questions.

On LeetCode (especially the [30 Days of JavaScript](https://leetcode.com/explore/featured/card/30-days-of-javascript/) track), this pattern shows up again and again. The skeleton stays the same — only the **leaf** and **branch** logic changes.

| Node type | What it is | What you do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Leaf** | Primitive (`number`, `string`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`) | Handle directly — compare, format, push, or return |
| **Branch** | `Array` or `Object` | Loop children, recurse, assemble result from returned values |

### 1. Flattening — the "smash it flat" pattern

Instead of keeping the nested shape, bring every leaf up to the top level.

- [LeetCode 2625 — Flatten Deeply Nested Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/flatten-deeply-nested-array/) (e.g. `[1, [2, [3]]]` → `[1, 2, 3]`)
- Flatten nested dictionary (e.g. `{ a: { b: 1 } }` → `{ "a.b": 1 }`)

**How the framework adapts:**

- **Leaf:** push the primitive into a single, shared array/object
- **Branch:** pass that shared container down into recursive calls so every child adds to the **same pile**

### 2. Deep comparison — the "two trees" pattern

Traverse **two** structures at the same time to check if they are identical.

- [LeetCode 2628 — JSON Deep Equal](https://leetcode.com/problems/json-deep-equal/)

**How the framework adapts:**

- **Leaf:** if both nodes are primitives, return `val1 === val2`
- **Branch:** if both are objects/arrays, loop keys (or indices) and recurse: `deepEqual(obj1[key], obj2[key])`

### 3. Transformation — the "translation" pattern

Keep the same tree shape, but change the data inside (format keys, wrap values, stringify).

- Deep camelCase — convert `snake_case` API keys to `camelCase` for a JS frontend
- [LeetCode 2633 — Convert Object to JSON String](https://leetcode.com/problems/convert-object-to-json-string/)

**How the framework adapts:**

- **Leaf:** format the primitive (wrap strings in quotes, emit numbers as strings, etc.)
- **Branch:** when building the new object/array, transform the key if needed, then assign the recursively transformed value

### 4. Diffing / merging — the "conflict resolution" pattern

Given two trees, combine them or find exactly what changed between version A and version B.

- [LeetCode 2700 — Differences Between Two Objects](https://leetcode.com/problems/differences-between-two-objects/)
- Deep merge — common in React/Redux when merging a state update into existing state

**How the framework adapts:**

- **Leaf:** if primitives differ, return `[oldValue, newValue]` (or pick the merge winner)
- **Branch:** if both are branches, dive deeper; if one is a branch and the other is a leaf (type changed), treat it as a difference

## Common mistakes

### 1. Check the value, not the key

Use `Boolean(value)`, not `Boolean(key)`. Property names like `"0"` or `"a"` are always truthy strings — you must test the **data** stored at that key.

```javascript
// Wrong — key is always truthy
if (Boolean(key)) { ... }

// Right — test the stored value
if (Boolean(value)) { ... }
```

### 2. Don't `delete` from arrays

Use `Array.isArray` + `.push()` so the result stays dense (`[1, 2]`). `delete arr[1]` leaves a hole (`[1, empty, 2]`).

```javascript
// Wrong — sparse array
if (Boolean(value)) compactedArr[i] = transform(value);
delete compactedArr[1];

// Right — dense array
if (Boolean(value)) compactedArr.push(transform(value));
```

### 3. Guard `null` first

`typeof null === 'object'`. Without an early `node === null` check, `for...in` on `null` throws.

```javascript
if (node === null) return node;           // before typeof check
if (typeof node !== 'object') return node;
```

## Top-down / bottom-up trace

Calls travel **down** the tree; return values travel **up**, each level building a new container from what came back below.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant root as transform(root)
  participant nested as transform(nested)
  participant leaf as transform(leaf)

  root->>nested: recurse into child
  nested->>leaf: recurse into inner value
  leaf-->>nested: return processed leaf
  Note over nested: bottom-up: assemble new container
  nested-->>root: return new nested structure
  Note over root: bottom-up: assemble root container
  root-->>root: return final result
```

Illustrative tree (labels only — one real-world case is [LeetCode 2705 — Compact Object](https://leetcode.com/problems/compact-object/)):

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  rootObj["{ a, b }"]
  rootObj --> valA["a: falsy → skip"]
  rootObj --> arrB["b: array"]
  arrB --> valFalse["false → skip"]
  arrB --> valOne["1 → keep, recurse"]
  valOne --> retOne["returns 1"]
  retOne --> newArr["bottom-up: [1]"]
  newArr --> newObj["bottom-up: { b: [1] }"]
```

Walkthrough in words:

1. **Down:** root object → nested array → leaf primitive `1`
2. **Up:** `1` returns → `[1]` is built → `{ b: [1] }` is assembled; falsy `a` was skipped at the object level

## Reference application

See [LeetCode 2705 — Compact Object](https://leetcode.com/problems/compact-object/) for a problem that applies this pattern: recursively remove falsy values from nested objects and arrays.

## The big takeaway

Whenever an interviewer hands you a problem involving unknown depths of arrays and objects, immediately think:

> "Okay, I need my **base case** for the primitive leaves, and a **loop with a recursive call** for the array/object branches."

Once you write that skeleton, you just fill in the specific logic for that exact problem — flatten, compare, transform, diff, or compact.

## Interview follow-ups

- **In-place vs rebuild** — when is mutation acceptable? (Usually avoid on interview tree problems; immutable rebuild is clearer and avoids array holes.)
- **`filter` + `map` vs explicit recursion** — functional one-liners work when shape is uniform; explicit loops clarify base cases and container type (array vs object).
- **Recognizing tree-shaped inputs** — nested JSON from `JSON.parse`, DOM-like configs, file system trees
- **`typeof null` trap** — always handle `null` before the generic object branch
